beats.say: A razor sells itself. And you never buy the razor again.
The starter is a single handle you keep forever.
The next tier adds a handful of replacement blades.
The top tier bundles the handle with a year's supply of blades.
The cheap handle looks like a one-time deal. Looks generous.
But it does a job - it forces you to keep buying blades.
You buy the handle once, then the blade-only option drives the bulk of sales.
In 1904 Gillette sold 90,884 handles but 123,648 blades - the refill dwarfs the starter.
That imbalance means the company earns forever from each customer.
You see it everywhere: a barber offers a basic shave, a premium styling, or a monthly blade refill.
A café sells a single coffee, a latte upgrade, or a bean-a-month subscription.
A gym lists a day pass, a class pack, or a yearly equipment lease - the recurring option feels like the smart choice.
Watch for a cheap starter that hides a forever-cost. Follow for more.
